Article Title: 'Why is BJP so worried?' Akhilesh gives fresh PDA definition amid Ayodhya visit attack
Article Text:
Akhilesh Yadav hits back at BJP over his proposed Ayodhya Ram temple visit

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday hit back at the BJP over its criticism of his proposed December 12 visit to the Ram temple in Ayodhya , asking why the ruling party was worried about the PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) outreach."God belongs to everyone. So why should we not visit these places? We will visit Kedareshwar, Mathura and Vrindavan as well. We have been visiting these places before, and we will continue to do so," Yadav said.Giving a fresh interpretation to the PDA acronym, he said, "PDA: Pehle darshan, phir Aashirvaad. So why is the BJP so worried about the PDA?" He added that his family already had the blessings of Shiv and Ram Gopal.Turning the attack towards the BJP, Yadav questioned what answer it had for the alleged large-scale corruption and destruction in the state, and the loss of lakhs of crores of rupees."In our family, Shiv and Ram Gopal are already there. We already have their blessings. So the BJP should not be worried. The question is, what answer does the BJP have for the massive loot and destruction that has taken place, and for the loss of lakhs of crores of rupees?..."he said.His remarks came after Uttar Pradesh BJP president Pankaj Chaudhary challenged Yadav to visit the Ram temple on December 6 instead of December 12 and apologise for the killing of kar sevaks during the SP government's tenure.Chaudhary alleged that Yadav's proposed visit was a political ploy and asked him to repent for what he described as the SP's past actions. BJP MLC Subhash Yaduvansh also asked the SP chief to apologise to kar sevaks and their families before visiting the shrine.Yadav's proposed December 12 visit would be his first to the Ram temple since its consecration in January 2024. The exchange comes months ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections.
Article Summary: Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav hit back at the BJP over its criticism of his proposed December 12 visit to the Ram temple in Ayodhya. Yadav asked why the ruling party was worried about the PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) outreach. He added that his family already had the blessings of Shiv and Ram Gopal.

Article Title: Kulgam terror attack: Terrorists were on motorcycle, search operation launched - what we know so far
Article Text:
Three security personnel injured in attack by terrorists in Kulgam

Here's what we know so far:

CRPF releases statement, says two injured

Recent attack on CRPF personnel in Chhattisgarh

NEW DELHI: Terrorists riding a motorcycle opened fire on Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) personnel deployed at a checkpoint in Jammu and Kashmir 's Kulgam district on Wednesday afternoon, injuring three security personnel. A search operation has been launched to track down the attackers.A CRPF official said that two of the three injured personnel were stable, while the third was in critical condition.The incident took place at around 2.15 pm when the assailants, riding a motorcycle, fired at the CRPF personnel before fleeing the spot, officials said. The injured personnel were shifted to a hospital in Anantnag district for treatment.Post attack, CRPF released a statement confirming that two personnel were injured."Two Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) personnel were injured after unidentified motorcycle-borne assailants opened fire on security personnel deployed at a naka in Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir this afternoon. The incident took place at around 2.15 pm when the assailants fired at the CRPF personnel before fleeing the spot.The injured personnel were shifted to a hospital in Anantnag district for treatment," it said.Last month, four CRPF personnel were injured in an accidental explosion while defusing residual explosives at the Alarmedgu camp in Chhattisgarh's Sukma district.The injured personnel belonged to the Ammunition Technician Team of the CRPF's 50th Battalion. They were inspecting camps in the Konta Range and disposing of unserviceable or residual explosives when a fragment of an explosive device detonated.
Article Summary: Terrorists riding a motorcycle opened fire on Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) personnel deployed at a checkpoint in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam district. A search operation has been launched to track down the attackers. A CRPF official said that two of the three injured personnel were stable, while the third was in critical condition.

Article Title: 'Things will be known at appropriate time': Sunetra Pawar on NCP merger speculation
Article Text:

(With PTI inputs)

NEW DELHI: Maharashtra deputy chief minister and Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) president Sunetra Pawar on Wednesday sidestepped a question on the possible merger of the party’s two factions, saying a decision would become clear at the “appropriate time”.“I know all of you are more interested in a different issue at present. However, today’s subject is entirely different. Things (about the merger) will be known when the time comes,” she told reporters in Baramati, the Pawar family’s political stronghold.The NCP, co-founded by veteran politician Sharad Pawar in 1999, split in July 2023 after his nephew, Ajit Pawar , broke away and joined the BJP-led ruling coalition in Maharashtra. The Election Commission subsequently recognised the Ajit Pawar-led faction as the "real" NCP, while the Sharad Pawar-led group was named the NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar).In January, the two factions contested the Maharashtra municipal corporation elections in alliance, fuelling speculation about a possible merger. However, Ajit Pawar’s death in a private plane crash later that month cast uncertainty over the prospects of reunification.Speculation about a possible merger gathered momentum last week after several NCP leaders, including Ajit and Sunetra Pawar’s son Parth and senior NCP leader Praful Patel, met Sharad Pawar, who was recently hospitalised with a chest infection.A video that went viral showed Sharad Pawar and Patel discussing a possible meeting after November 10.NCP state president Sunil Tatkare also claimed last week that the merger would have taken place in February if Ajit Pawar had not died.Ajit Pawar, who was Maharashtra’s deputy chief minister and NCP president, died in a private plane crash on January 28. Sunetra Pawar subsequently took over as the party’s president and became deputy chief minister in the BJP-led Maharashtra government, which also includes the Shiv Sena.
Article Summary: NCP split in July 2023 after Ajit Pawar broke away and joined the BJP-led ruling coalition in Maharashtra. In January, the two factions contested the Maharashtra municipal corporation elections in alliance, fuelling speculation about a possible merger. Ajit Pawar’s death in a private plane crash later that month cast uncertainty over the prospects of reunification.

Article Title: 'Anti-people': Karnataka BJP stages protest against Congress over price hikes including milk
Article Text:
BJP stages protest in Karnataka against milk price hike and rising transport costs, accusing the Congress government of burdening the common man

NEW DELHI: The Bharatiya Janata Party's Karnataka unit staged a protest against Congress government on Wednesday criticising the recent price hikes, including that of milk in the state. The state government's decided to hike milk prices by up to Rs 8 per litre, along with increases in bus fares and other transport costs.Former Karnataka chief minister Basavaraj Bommai claimed that over Rs 1 lakh crore in new taxes had been levied on the people of Karnataka."From day one, they are increasing the price of all commodities, of all services, including land revenue. And it has gone to the sky high. The other day they increased rent. They increased water. They increased flour. They increased diesel. They have increased alcohol. They have increased all the taxes. So, almost more than one lakh crore in new tax has been levied on the people of Karnataka," news agency ANI quoted him as saying."And other than this, they have taken a four lakh cr loan in the last three years. So it’s a heavy burden on the people of Karnataka. That’s why BJP has been protesting all along. And today they are making a protest against all the price rises done by the state government. This is an anti-people government and anti-development government," he added.Former chief minister and BJP leader BS Yediyurappa joined the protest, criticising the price hikes and highlighting the burden they have placed on the public."It's very difficult for the common man that one cup of tea. They are raising it by about 10-12 rupees. The common man suffered lot. Not only milk, even bus charges also they have raised and bus luggage also they have raised," news agency ANI quoted him as saying."So it shows that this government not all bothered about the common man. So that's why we are seeing dharna today. We are protesting. I will demand chief minister to withdraw all this unnecessary rise of price price rise," he added.The protest was led by BJP state president B Y Vijayendra, leader of opposition in the legislative assembly R Ashoka and leader of opposition in the legislative council Chalavadi Narayanaswamy. BJP workers raised slogans against the Congress government, condemning the recent hikes in milk prices and bus fares.The protesters accused the state government, led by D K Shivakumar, of burdening ordinary people with successive price increases and described it as an "anti-people government".
Article Summary: Bharatiya Janata Party's Karnataka unit staged a protest against Congress government on Wednesday. The state government's decided to hike milk prices by up to Rs 8 per litre, along with increases in bus fares and other transport costs. The protesters accused the state government of burdening ordinary people with successive price increases.

Article Title: 'Let us have a debate': Akhilesh Yadav challenges BJP over demonetisation
Article Text:
File photo: SP chief Akhilesh Yadav

Yadav alleges damage to banks, MSMEs

Centre cites tax action after demonetisation

Yogi Adityanath targets SP over recruitment

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday renewed his criticism of the 2016 demonetisation exercise, calling it the "biggest corruption scandal in the world" and alleging that it had damaged banks, small traders and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).Addressing a press conference in Lucknow, Yadav invoked his "Khajanchi" jibe against demonetisation, marking 10 years of the child associated with his criticism of the currency ban.He said the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) should adopt Khajanchi and celebrate his birthday, while accusing the party of failing to acknowledge the consequences of the policy."Today Khajanchi turned 10. We have been celebrating its birthday since the beginning, but sadly the Bharatiya Janata Party has never celebrated Khajanchi's birthday. Bharatiya Janata Party should adopt it, but not how their MPs adopted villages," Yadav said.He alleged that demonetisation had increased cash circulation and described the exercise as "slow poison" for the economy. He also claimed that the move had been intended to "sink the banks".The SP chief questioned the government's banking reforms, including the merger and privatisation of banks, and alleged that demonetisation had weakened the banking system."The circulation of cash has increased by 70 per cent compared to what it was earlier. There is a long list of the damage that has been caused to MSMEs and small traders," he said.Yadav also criticised banks for deducting money from customers in the form of penalties, alleging that the banking system had become more difficult to navigate than dealing with moneylenders."Demonetisation became a curse for banks. Banks themselves were shut down, banks were merged, and even banks had to be sold," he said.He challenged the government to debate India's economic position at the time of Independence in 1947 and its stated ambition of becoming a developed country by 2047."The truth is that these people keep throwing around the slogan of a developed India by 2047. One negative decision like demonetisation has pushed India's economy even further behind the economic position we had in 1947, when we became independent," Yadav said."If they feel these allegations are not true, let us have a debate on this as well. Let there be a debate on what the economic situation was in 1947 and what it will be in 2047, and how far they have pushed us backwards," he added.The Centre announced the withdrawal of the old Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 currency notes on November 8, 2016, saying the move was aimed at tackling tax evasion and black money.The government has maintained that the exercise was successful in increasing the number of income tax returns filed.According to the finance ministry, the Income Tax Department conducted search and seizure operations against 900 groups between November 2016 and March 2017. These actions resulted in the seizure of Rs 900 crore, including cash worth Rs 636 crore, and the admission of undisclosed income of about Rs 7,961 crore.Opposition parties have repeatedly questioned whether demonetisation achieved its stated objectives.Yadav's remarks came amid a fresh exchange between the Samajwadi Party and the BJP in Uttar Pradesh. Chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Wednesday accused the SP and the Congress of corruption, nepotism and irregularities in government recruitment before 2017.Speaking at a programme for distributing appointment letters to 1,146 newly selected junior assistants in the Revenue Department, Adityanath alleged that a "Saifai syndicate" had controlled recruitment commissions and boards under previous governments.Without naming Yadav, the chief minister took aim at the SP chief over his criticism of the government's announcement on distributing appointment letters to one lakh young people.Adityanath alleged that candidates had been cheated through recruitment irregularities, with some paying money to secure jobs while others lost out despite preparing for examinations. He also claimed that around 1.5 lakh police posts were vacant when his government took office in 2017.The chief minister accused previous SP governments of lawlessness and said Uttar Pradesh had since seen improvements in law and order, employment opportunities and business activity.
Article Summary: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav renews his criticism of the 2016 demonetisation exercise. Yadav alleges that it had damaged banks, small traders and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) He said the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) should celebrate Khajanchi's birthday.

Article Title: 'She's like a statesman': Robert Vadra urges BJP leaders to read Sonia Gandhi's memoir
Article Text:
Vadra described Sonia's decision to nominate Manmohan Singh for the PM post as “a very wise decision”.

NEW DELHI: Sonia Gandhi’s son-in-law and businessman Robert Vadra on Wednesday urged BJP leaders to read the Congress parliamentary party chairperson’s memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, with an “open mind”.“I would say that the BJP people should learn from Mrs Gandhi. I would say that they should read the book with an open mind. She's like a statesman and she's like a mentor to many people,” Vadra said, speaking to news agency ANI.Vadra said he was proud of his mother-in-law and the experiences she had shared in the book, which he received from her on Tuesday. He said he was yet to read the memoir but intended to do so.“I'm very proud of my mother-in-law for her life, her experience, my relationship with her, what I've learned from her, how she takes care of everything. And definitely all of that and more is in the book. Though I'll say that I still haven't read the book, but I'm a proud owner of the book which I received yesterday from her,” he said.Vadra also revealed that Sonia Gandhi had personally dedicated the book to him.“She mentioned she wrote a little something for me, that 'to my son-in-law Robert with lots of love, your mom-in-law'.”“So it's a personal book for me which I'm going to definitely read,” he said.He said the memoir took 12 years to complete and drew on her real-life experiences. Vadra described her as a woman who had shown strength and resilience while dealing with difficulties and making important decisions.“She's always had a lot of strength, resilience and energy to deal with everything every day,” he said.Referring to her move to India after marrying into the Gandhi family, Vadra said she had shown considerable commitment and strength.“She's a strong, sincere lady with a lot of experience, a lot of commitment that she learned when she gave up her life and she got married and came to this country. And coming to the Gandhi family requires a lot of strength,” he said.Vadra also recalled Sonia Gandhi's support during his questioning by the Enforcement Directorate (ED). Alleging that he had faced false accusations and repeated summons, he said she would wait for him after each interrogation to check on his well-being.“Every time I returned from my interrogation, I saw my mother-in-law was there waiting for me to see how I'm doing. Her experience really helped, and it gave me the strength to deal with anything which was even false that I had to deal with,” he said.Defending Sonia Gandhi's decision to decline the prime minister's post after the 2004 Lok Sabha elections, Vadra said she was not seeking political power. He described her decision to nominate Manmohan Singh for the post as “a very wise decision”.He said people respected her for not pursuing positions and for wanting the country to remain secular and develop as a society.
Article Summary: Sonia Gandhi’s son-in-law and businessman Robert Vadra on Wednesday urged BJP leaders to read the Congress parliamentary party chairperson's memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love. Vadra described Sonia's decision to nominate Manmohan Singh for the PM post as “a very wise decision”

Article Title: Three workers killed during water tank maintenance at Tata iPhone parts factory in Tamil Nadu
Article Text:
Three workers died in an incident at Tata Electronics' facility in Hosur, Tamil Nadu.

NEW DELHI: Three contract workers died on Monday evening after drowning while carrying out maintenance and cleaning work inside a nano-filtration feed tank at Tata Marigold Company in Vanniyapuram, Krishnagiri district, Tamil Nadu The deceased were identified as Kaveri, 28, J Akmal, 28, and Sarath Kumar, 25, all residents of Rayakottai. They were cleaning the tank when the incident occurred.“They were immediately rescued and rushed to a nearby hospital. However, doctors declared them brought dead,” Krishnagiri district collector C Dinesh Kumar said.State minister Virudhai Magal Keerthana expressed grief over the deaths and said she had spoken to the district administration to ensure support for the affected families.“Deeply saddened by the tragic loss of three precious lives in the incident at Tata Electronics' facility in Hosur...I have spoken to the district administration and directed them to extend all necessary support to the affected families and ensure that the situation is addressed with utmost urgency,” she said.“The safety and dignity of every worker must remain paramount. This tragic incident will be thoroughly investigated, and appropriate action will be taken based on the findings.We must ensure that every necessary measure is put in place to prevent such tragedies from recurring,” the minister added.Authorities have launched an inquiry to establish the circumstances leading to the incident and determine whether there were any lapses in industrial safety protocols at the facility. Rayakottai police have registered a case and initiated an investigation. The district administration and police are also monitoring the situation around the industrial unit to maintain law and order.Following an update on the probe from Apple, the company's team visited the Tata factory to investigate the incident, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters.Tata Electronics, an Apple supplier, has also reportedly been instructed to conduct a comprehensive review of the performance and safety compliance of the agencies responsible for maintaining the Effluent Treatment Plant (ETP).
Article Summary: Three contract workers died on Monday evening after drowning while carrying out maintenance and cleaning work inside a nano-filtration feed tank at Tata Marigold Company in Vanniyapuram, Krishnagiri district, Tamil Nadu. Authorities have launched an inquiry to establish the circumstances leading to the incident. Apple has also reportedly been instructed to conduct a comprehensive review of the performance and safety compliance of the agencies responsible for maintaining the Effluent Treatment Plant.

Article Title: Hasina seeks passport, Dhaka calls it political stunt & seeks extradition
Article Text:
Kobir said there is no scope now for staging drama in the name of returning to the country using the passport issue (Photo: Reuters).

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

DHAKA/NEW DELHI: India-Bangladesh ties may experience fresh turbulence with ousted PM Sheikh Hasina 's legal counsel formally requesting a new passport and national identity card from the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to facilitate her return to the country. While the high commission said it wasn't sure if the request was genuine as it was not backed by supporting documents, Dhaka responded by declaring it doesn't issue passports to "convicted terrorists" and reiterating its demand for Hasina's extradition.India, however, sees the passport request as a matter purely between the government in Dhaka and a Bangladeshi national, one that should not be conflated with her extradition issue. The Indian government maintains that Hasina's extradition is subject to established legal and judicial processes under the bilateral extradition treaty.Hasina had earlier announced that she planned to 'return' to Bangladesh in December. However, India is likely to distance itself from Hasina's passport bid - described by Bangladesh authorities as a political stunt - as it believes this will be Dhaka's call entirely."She has fled after killing people. One who has fled, how would she come? How would a terrorist come? There’s an extradition treaty. Handover would be sought through the treaty," said Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir.Kobir said there is no scope now for staging drama in the name of returning to the country using the passport issue.“If she truly wishes to return, there is a specific legal process for doing so. An extradition treaty exists between Bangladesh and India; she should ask the Indian government to hand her over to Bangladesh under the terms of that treaty. She should return, surrender to the court, and serve her sentence,” he said.Political insiders in Dhaka say the government and opposition party Jamaat do not actually want Hasina’s return at this moment and that is why the government is unwilling to accept her voluntary return and tagging extradition treaty issue which is time-consuming and complicated.In 2025, a Bangladeshi special tribunal sentenced her to death for crimes against humanity, ruling that she was responsible for ordering the crackdown, which left hundreds of people dead and thousands of others injured.Hasina requested a new passport on Monday to facilitate her return from exile two years after she was ousted in a mass uprising.In a letter, emailed to the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, Hasina’s counsel urged the top diplomat to take necessary action to provide her with a passport and national identity card.The letter, sent by London-based law firm Matrix Chambers, asked the mission for the application to be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of Hasina’s Bangladeshi nationality and in accordance with “obligations arising under international human rights instruments.”The letter, sent via email and addressed to Acting High Commissioner Preeti Rahman, was shared with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.Hasina’s application is ridiculous, State Minister Kobir said, criticising the British law firm over its involvement in the matter.“Know your client. Don’t run after her looted money from the people of Bangladesh. Exercise some ethical and moral boundaries. And if you don’t have those boundaries, you will be shamed all over the world,” he said.“If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” Hasina told AP in response to questions by email. “So, I will return to Bangladesh. That decision has not changed.”
Article Summary: Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina's legal counsel formally requested a new passport and national identity card from the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi. Dhaka responded by declaring it doesn't issue passports to "convicted terrorists" India, however, sees the passport request as a matter purely between the government in Dhaka and a Bangladeshi national.

Article Title: Ahead of peace talks, Zelenskyy seeks PM Modi's help on ceasefire
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke Monday

NEW DELHI: Ahead of the Abu Dhabi peace talks, PM Narendra Modi and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke Monday with the latter briefing the PM about latest developments related to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and Modi conveying India’s "firm commitment" to contributing in every possible way towards a peaceful resolution of the Russia-Ukraine war.The conversation took place a day before the trilateral peace dialogue involving Russia, Ukraine and the US in Abu Dhabi, and amid renewed Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. Ahead of the talks, where India's recent peace proposals are likely to be discussed too, India remained engaged with both sides on diplomatic initiatives as foreign minister S Jaishankar too spoke to his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov.Zelenskyy recalled Modi's latest peace message to President Vladimir Putin that it was time now to end the "endless war" and urged India to take more steps towards a ceasefire that can ensure food and energy security. Modi said in a post on X that he and Zelenskyy had a productive conversation – their first since they met on the margins of the G7 summit in France in June.Modi's message to Zelenskyy expressing India's readiness to facilitate peace is not new, but its timing is significant as this was the first time they spoke after Jaishankar revealed in early October India was actively mediating for establishment of safe corridors in the Black Sea for grain and energy exports."We reviewed our wide-ranging bilateral cooperation and agreed to further strengthen India-Ukraine ties. I thanked President Zelenskyy for sharing his perspectives on the ongoing conflict, its humanitarian aspects and various efforts to restore peace," said Modi in his own readout of the talks.Ukraine believes Russia has not responded positively to India's Black Sea shipping proposal and the call to end targeting of its energy sector. "The Prime Minister has said more than once, including directly to the Russian ‌leader, ⁠that now is the time to end the war, not to continue it," said Zelenskyy on X after his talks with Modi, urging India to identify steps it can take and also talks it can pursue with other leaders to bring the conflict to an end.“Food security could be one such area. We discussed Russia's blocking of grain exports via the Black Sea. India is ready to mediate in establishing food corridors, and we are counting on these efforts to continue,” said the Ukrainian president.Zelenskyy also said Ukraine had always taken a constructive approach, and Russia must show the same readiness to de-escalate.“Russia must understand that the global economy and hundreds of millions of people around the world are suffering because of blocked sea routes. We agreed that our teams will stay in touch on these and other bilateral issues,” he said.An Indian readout said Modi reaffirmed India’s human-centric approach and reiterated India’s consistent position that the conflict must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.The 4th round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks mediated by the US are scheduled to begin in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. While the core negotiations are structured as trilateral sessions involving Russia, Ukraine, and the US, Ukrainian delegation will hold separate coordination meetings with their European and Nato allies including France, Germany and the UK on the sidelines.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke Monday ahead of the Abu Dhabi peace talks. The conversation took place a day before the trilateral peace dialogue involving Russia, Ukraine and the US in Abu Dhabi. India's recent peace proposals are likely to be discussed too.

Article Title: What made Sonia Gandhi turn down PM post after UPA’s 2004 victory? Memoir revisits moment
Article Text:
After deciding against taking the top post, Sonia had to identify someone who could lead the new government. She says several senior Congress leaders were qualified for the position, but Manmohan Singh stood out.

'Sonia, be true to yourself': What made her change her mind

What else Sonia Gandhi's memoir cover

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi has revealed what went through her mind when she decided against becoming prime minister after the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) won the 2004 Lok Sabha elections.In her newly released memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia recalls how she eventually listened to her "inner voice" and decided to turn down the top post, despite initially being expected to lead the government. She also explains why she chose Manmohan Singh to become prime minister, describing him as a leader of "unquestionable" integrity with a deep understanding of governance.The memoi revisits the crucial political decision that shaped the UPA government's first term. Sonia also shares details of the discussions with senior Congress leaders and her final conversation with her son, Rahul Gandhi, before announcing her decision.Also Read| 'I'd quake in my seat': Sonia Gandhi recalls Indira Gandhi's temper, early days as bride in memoir Sharing an excerpt from the memoir in an article published by The Indian Express, Sonia Gandhi recalled the moment she finally resolved not to become prime minister."My mind suddenly cleared itself of the last shreds of doubt. “Sonia, be true to yourself,” I could hear myself say.“You’ve always known it. Just leave it!” From Belonging - on the decision not to become Prime Minister," she wrote in a post on X.In the book, she describes how she woke up a few hours later and went straight to Rahul's room to tell him about her decision."I woke up in a few hours, went straight to my son’s room, and knocked on the door. “I’ve made up my mind. I’m going to stick to my stand,” I told him. He stepped up to me and with his arms around me said, “It’s the right decision.”"The CPP President also recalls returning to the Congress Parliamentary Party meeting after making up her mind."I enter the hall to thunderous applause. The members of Par­liament stand up in their places, thumping their palms on the wooden ledges in front of them. I find my place at the centre of the long table for the leaders of the party and remain standing till someone gestures for them to stop, and we all take our seats," she wrote.Also Read| 'Should've called it Whitewashing, not Belonging': BJP mocks Sonia Gandhi's memoir After deciding against taking the top post, Sonia had to identify someone who could lead the new government. She says several senior Congress leaders were qualified for the position, but Manmohan Singh stood out."There were several senior colleagues, seasoned and qualified for the post, who would have been more than willing to accept it but amongst all of them was one who had long been in my sight as a person above reproach, and possessed a deep and consummate understanding of governance. That was Dr Manmohan Singh, a member of the Congress Working Committee," she writes.Sonia points to Singh's experience as finance minister in the early 1990s, when he introduced economic reforms under the government of then prime minister PV Narasimha Rao.She also believed his appointment would reassure people about the UPA's economic policies, particularly as the alliance was supported by the Communist parties."He was not allied to any camp in the party. Over a period of time, the Congress had been painted as being left of centre, and our government would now be supported by the Communist parties as well. I thought Dr Manmohan Singh would assuage the doubts of many about our ability to manage and continue the policies that had been begun years ago," she says.Sonia also recalls Manmohan Singh's personal journey, from a village in Punjab, now in Pakistan, to the universities of Oxford and Cambridge. She describes him as a hardworking scholar and technocrat who had overcome considerable hardship."Aside from all his accomplishments as a scholar and technocrat, what I knew best about Dr Singh was that he had a kind and compassionate heart, and his integrity unquestionable," she writes.She says she was convinced that the country would be in safe hands under his leadership. After consulting senior colleagues, she proposed his name. They did not oppose the choice.Manmohan Singh was approached privately about taking up the position. Although he initially declined, the CPP President says he was eventually persuaded to accept it.Sonia Gandhi also recounts the events of May 18, 2004, when she went to Rashtrapati Bhawan to stake the UPA's claim to form the government. She was accompanied by Singh.Recalling her arrival, she describes an emotional moment as she walked through the building where she had earlier visited with her mother-in-law, former prime minister Indira Gandhi, and her husband, Rajiv Gandhi."I felt a sudden surge of emotion as our cars pulled up at the entrance. I'd been there many times before with my mother-in-law and with Rajiv, but this time I was walking through the long, dark corridors of Rashtrapati Bhawan for a different purpose," she writes.After the meeting, the two returned to her residence at 10, Janpath. Sonia Gandhi says she did not discuss the prime ministership with Singh, who, like everyone else, assumed she would take the post."We returned from Rashtrapati Bhawan to my home at 10, Janpath. I saw Dr Singh to his car. There had been no discussion about the prime ministership between the two of us on the drive back nor had there been before that. I said nothing to him even now. He had quite naturally assumed, like everyone else, that it would be me," she recalls.Sonia Gandhi has recalled how Pranab Mukherjee hinted at his "long-held desire" to become prime minister during a 2010 conversation, when he suggested that "it was time for a change at the top", according to her newly released memoir.Rejecting criticism that she was a "back seat driver" during the UPA years, Sonia said she respected Manmohan Singh's position as prime minister and believed it was her duty to defer to him, even when they disagreed."Further. I was determined not to be under any circumstance the cause of a misunderstanding that could give our opponents occasion to rejoice and weaken our government," she writes in the book, released on Tuesday.Also Read| ‘Not a political book, but a personal one’: Sonia Gandhi ahead of memoir release Belonging: A Journey of Love traces Sonia Gandhi's life from her childhood in post-war Italy to her marriage to Rajiv Sonia Gandhi and her eventual move to India.Born in Italy, she was 19 and studying in Cambridge, England, when she met Rajiv in 1965. The couple married on February 25, 1968. The memoir recounts her introduction to Indira Gandhi and her efforts to adjust to life in India, including learning Hindi, wearing saris and adapting to Indian food and culture.It also revisits the personal tragedies that shaped her life, including the death of Sanjay Gandhi in a plane crash, Indira Gandhi's assassination in 1984 and Rajiv Gandhi's assassination in 1991.Among the most personal accounts is her recollection of the night Rajiv was assassinated in Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu, on May 21, 1991. She recalls how their daughter Priyanka broke the news to her and how she struggled to accept that her husband was dead.The memoir also recounts Rahul's concerns about his father's security. Two months before the assassination, Rahul had warned his mother: "If something isn’t done about Pa’s security, I know I’ll soon have to come back for his funeral."
Article Summary: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi has revealed what went through her mind when she decided against becoming prime minister. In her newly released memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia recalls how she eventually listened to her "inner voice" and decided to turn down the top post. She also explains why she chose Manmohan Singh to become prime minister, describing him as a leader of "unquestionable" integrity.

Article Title: Person has no claim in grandpa's property held by dad, says SC
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Can a grandson claim a share in property inherited by his father from his grandfather? Supreme Court has ruled that a person becomes the absolute owner of his share in his father's ancestral or self-acquired property and can deal with it exclusively, including excluding his sons.Ending a 29-year legal battle, a bench of Justices Augustine George Masih and Sunita Agarwal rejected a son's plea for partition of his father's property. The son had filed the suit in 1997, claiming the property was ancestral or joint family property. The court said a son's son is not listed as a Class I heir under the Hindu Succession Act and cannot claim a share in his grandfather's property.Referring to Section 8, which lays down succession rules when a Hindu male dies intestate, the bench said a son becomes the absolute owner of property inherited from his father, while his own son has no right by birth over it.SC said Class I heirs inherit simultaneously, to the exclusion of all others. "A son's son is not mentioned as an heir under Class I of the Schedule, and, therefore, he could not get any right in the property of his grandfather," it said.It added that 1956 law did not preserve right under personal Hindu law of a grandson to claim a share in his grandfather's property during his father's lifetime. Sec 8 must be read as a self-contained provision governing devolution of property of a Hindu male dying intestate, it said.Citing SC judgements, the bench rejected the argument that a son inheriting property under Section 8 holds it as karta of his undivided family. Such an interpretation would create two classes among Class I heirs, treating property as joint family property for male heirs but not female heirs, it said. The express wording of Sec 8 must prevail.Upholding HC's order, the bench said a grandson cannot seek partition of property held by his father. The high court had ruled that when a son or daughter receives property through partition, whether ancestral or self-acquired, they become absolute owners of their shares and can deal with them exclusively, including excluding their sons.
Article Summary: Supreme Court rejects son's plea for partition of his father's property. The son had filed the suit in 1997, claiming the property was ancestral or joint family property. Court said a son's son is not listed as a Class I heir under the Hindu Succession Act.

NEW DELHI: Sonia Gandhi 's memoirs, released on Tuesday, officially acknowledge what was long whispered within political circles but never publicly confirmed - her battle with cancer, which occurred during the second term of UPA govt.They also set the record straight on where her two surgeries took place - first at European Institute of Oncology, near Milan in Italy, and later at Erasmus University Medical Centre in Rotterdam - and not at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, as was widely speculated.According to Sonia , while she had suffered from occasional bouts of asthma and allergies, she had no serious health troubles until 2010, when she was advised to undergo surgery for suspected breast cancer. She chose not to get operated on in India as she wanted to avoid a media frenzy.After much discussion with her doctors, Sonia Gandhi opted to get operated on by Dr Veronesi, a celebrated surgeon who was the founder and head of the European Institute.In her book, ‘Belonging: A Journey of Love’, Sonia writes, “On the day of the surgery, as I was wheeled into the operation theatre, Rahul and Priyanka held my hand and kissed me on the forehead, assuring me that all would be well.Afterwards, still groggy from the anaesthesia, I saw Dr Veronesi with them by my bedside. How relieved I felt to hear him announce, ‘Non c’è niente da preoccuparsi, tutto è andato bene e non ci sono residui. (No need to worry, everything has gone well and there are no residues).’ He had removed two tumours, including a non-suspicious one to be on the safe side, and conducted an intra-operative radiation to spare me five weeks of radiotherapy. ”However, a year later, routine follow-up tests detected a growth in the pancreas. This time Sonia was sent to Erasmus, to be treated by a well-known pancreatic surgeon, Dr Casper van Eijck. Again, Rahul and Priyanka were by her side before the surgery. When she woke up, dazed and parched, she heard them calling out, “Ma, Mama, all is well — nothing bad!” The doctor later explained that fortunately, the tumour was found in a preliminary precancerous stage, having been detected early.Sonia also mentions that in Aug 2016, she collapsed during a long roadshow in hot and humid weather in Varanasi and broke her shoulder in the fall, forcing her to undergo another operation. While being flown to Delhi and floating in and out of consciousness, she writes, “Then I saw him again — Rajiv, reaching out to me, smiling at me reassuringly as if to say, ‘everything will be fine’; Sheila Dikshit , who was by my side throughout, told me later that she noticed me suddenly smile in the middle of the tension-racked flight — I’m sure it must have been that moment.”Apart from these episodes, there have been no other major health scares — though, like most residents of Delhi, the toxic winter air does bother her.
Article Summary: Sonia Gandhi's memoirs acknowledge what was long whispered within political circles but never publicly confirmed - her battle with cancer. They also set the record straight on where her two surgeries took place - first at European Institute of Oncology, near Milan in Italy, and later at Erasmus University Medical Centre in Rotterdam.

Article Title: 80% of Delhi's pollution Monday due to crackers

NEW DELHI: Firecracker emissions accounted for more than 80% of Delhi's pollution load on Monday, a day after Diwali , according to the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology's models, highlighting the sharp impact of fireworks on the capital's air quality. The contribution came even as the city was already battling high pollution levels from multiple sources.The situation, however, showed some improvement on Tuesday, with the AQI at 299 at 4pm, bringing it into the 'poor' category from 'very poor' a day earlier. However, it deteriorated to very poor by 6pm with an AQI of 302.Toxins from Diwali firecrackers lingered on Tuesday as well, with IITM showing 29.9% of pollution contribution due to firecrackers between 1am and 9am, while secondary organic compounds - formed due to chemical reactions of emitted particles in air - were the secondary source at 17.5% of net pollution on Tuesday. IMD attributed cleaner air to favourable wind, which helped disperse pollutants accumulated over the city and barred intrusion of stubble smoke from neighbouring states.The easing came despite a significant number of farm fires being reported in neighbouring Punjab. An assessment of the decision support system for air quality management indicated that stubble burning was not a major contributor to Delhi’s pollution load on Monday. This suggests that the immediate post-Diwali pollution spike was driven primarily by local fireworks rather than a major influx of crop-residue smoke.The high contribution from firecrackers followed a sharp deterioration in air quality during the festival. Delhi’s average AQI was 376 on Diwali, Nov 8, the highest recorded for the festival in five years. It remained in the ‘very poor’ category on Monday, with the city waking up to a thick layer of smog and several monitoring stations reporting severe air quality.IITM’s model estimates the contribution of different sources to the city’s particulate pollution a day after Diwali on Nov 9, including secondary organic compounds, at 5.8%, the second dominant source, and vehicular pollution at 4.4%, the third biggest source. However, the city’s air quality will depend on how effectively winds disperse the remaining pollutants and on emissions from routine sources.
Article Summary: Firecracker emissions accounted for more than 80% of Delhi's pollution load on Monday, a day after Diwali. The contribution came even as the city was already battling high pollution levels from multiple sources. The situation, however, showed some improvement on Tuesday, with the AQI at 299 at 4pm.

Article Title: CPCB explains why official AQI is capped at 500 despite private apps showing higher readings
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: The Central Pollution Control Board on Tuesday defended its air quality monitoring methodology, explaining why official AQI readings are capped at 500 even as private monitoring apps reported levels as high as 1,800 in Delhi after Diwali.The clarification came amid questions over the wide disparity between government data and readings displayed by private air quality monitoring platforms.The CPCB said the 500-point ceiling was an intentional feature of the National Air Quality Index (NAQI), consistent with international practices. It explained that readings beyond 500 would not change the health advisory, as all such levels fall under the 'Severe' category."The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a tool for effective communication of air quality status to the people in terms that are easy to understand. AQI is an indicative scale designed to convey the likely health implications of prevailing air quality conditions. The AQI category along with the associated health statement is more significant than the corresponding AQI value within that category," the board said in a statement.The CPCB said the official index uses scientifically validated 24-hour rolling averages to assess sustained exposure to pollutants. Private apps, on the other hand, often capture hourly fluctuations through low-cost sensors, which may show sharp spikes in pollution levels.According to the board, the NAQI has six categories - 'Good', 'Satisfactory', 'Moderately Polluted', 'Poor', 'Very Poor' and 'Severe' - within a scale of 0 to 500. It said an AQI reading of 500 or above indicates broadly similar health risks and therefore does not warrant a separate category."Beyond this level the AQI remains in the 'Severe' category and extrapolation of the index would not alter the assigned health impact category. The capping at 500 is thus a design feature of the index, as has been evolved in 2015 methodology of NAQI in line with the prevailing international practice including US EPA AQI scale," it added.CPCB also said private apps could report higher readings during brief pollution spikes but show lower figures when pollution levels subsequently decline."It is generally perceived that private apps show higher AQI. This may hold during short peaks, when hourly values rise sharply. However, when concentrations fall, such apps show lower AQI than the NAQI, since the NAQI continues to reflect the exposure of the preceding 24 hours," it said."This has also been evident in Delhi post Diwali firecrackers bursting event. The NAQI thus provides a consistent and reliable indication of the likely health impacts of sustained exposure to pollutants, which is the scientifically relevant measure for public health advisories," it further said.The clarification came as social media posts showing screenshots of private air quality apps reporting AQI levels between 1,500 and 1,800 in Delhi on Diwali night, while CPCB's official readings remained below 400.
Article Summary: The Central Pollution Control Board defended its air quality monitoring methodology. It said the 500-point ceiling was an intentional feature of the National Air Quality Index (NAQI) The board said readings beyond 500 would not change the health advisory, as all such levels fall under 'Severe' category.

Sonia recounts moments with world leaders in her memoir

Sarkozy's love life and an amused Sonia

NEW DELHI: Former Congress president Sonia Gandhi recalls in her memoir how then-US president Bill Clinton, during his 2000 India visit, would occasionally be seen "surreptitiously sizing up the more striking women" at a reception hosted in his honour. The Monica Lewinsky scandal may have faded from the headlines by then, but, as Sonia writes, "old habits die hard".The anecdote is among several candid recollections of Sonia's interactions with global leaders and prominent personalities, including former French president Nicolas Sarkozy and the late Princess Diana, in her newly released memoir, Belonging: A Journey Of Love.Recalling Clinton's 2000 visit, Sonia writes about meeting the then US president at the Sheraton hotel, where he was staying with his daughter Chelsea and his delegation. She had called on him along with then-foreign minister."Friendly, informal, and exuding confidence, he appeared more keen to give us his own views and predictions about Kashmir- 'a nuclear flashpoint', in his words, 'one of the most dangerous places on earth'--than to pay attention to our point of view," she writes.Sonia also recounts a reception hosted by then-prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee in Clinton's honour, where she noticed the former US president occasionally looking at women in attendance."The Monica Lewinsky scandal had subsided a little by then, but old habits die hard; at the reception held by Prime Minister Vajpayee in his honour, I noticed him every now and then surreptitiously sizing up the more striking women present," she writes.Sonia also shares an interesting account of Nicolas Sarkozy's 2008 visit to India, when the French president travelled without his then partner, Carla Bruni."It was said that he (Sarkozy) had been advised not to bring her (Bruni) because they were unmarried which would have been awkward at official functions," she writes.At a banquet, the wife of then vice-president Mohammad Ansari, seated next to Sarkozy, began asking him about his relationship with Bruni, including whether he planned to marry her and whether a date had been fixed."President Sarkozy seemed unperturbed by the cross-examination, even eager to share details of his love life, answering all her questions while continuously messaging his Carla on his phone," Sonia recalls.The couple made a joint appearance in India on a subsequent visit, attending a private dinner hosted by then prime minister Manmohan Singh and his wife.By then, Sarkozy and Bruni had married. Sonia remembers the French president as being visibly besotted with his wife, who had been a popular singer and songwriter in Europe as well as a top model."All eyes were on her as she glided into the room in an elegant long gown, graceful and slim, demure and blue-eyed," she writes.However, Sonia's impression of the evening was not limited to Bruni's appearance. She also recalls Sarkozy holding forth on India's responsibilities while speaking to Manmohan Singh."He was obviously besotted with his tall and beautiful wife of Italian and French descent, who had been a popular singer and songwriter in Europe, as well as a top model. All eyes were on her as she glided into the room in an elegant long gown, graceful and slim, demure and blue-eyed," she writes."She spoke cordially but infrequently--while her husband held forth, expounding his views to our prime minister on what India should do in what I felt was a rather arrogant manner, unmindful of the fact that he was talking to someone more senior, more experienced and more knowledgeable," she adds.Among the most personal recollections in the memoir are Sonia's encounters with the British royal family, particularly Princess Diana.She writes that members of the British royal family had shared a friendship with the Nehru-Gandhi family over generations, while Rajiv Gandhi had got along well with Prince Charles."The real star of that family had of course been Princess Diana: Tall and slim, with large blue eyes, an enchanting smile, and a magnetic personality. I can never forget how ravishing she was as a bride when Rajiv and I attended their wedding in 1981. But when they came to India in 1992, it was evident that things were not going well in the marriage," Sonia writes.She recalls an informal meeting with the royal couple during their 1992 India visit, on the same day Diana famously posed alone on a bench in front of the Taj Mahal, later popularly known as the 'love bench'."On the very day she famously posed alone on what I call the 'love bench' in front of the Taj Mahal, they had come over for a late tea. Prince Charles was forthcoming and amusing, but she appeared morose, though looking wonderful in a striking red and purple two-piece suit. We chatted about what she had seen and liked on her visit," she writes.Sonia's mother, who was visiting at the time, was keen to meet the princess. Her daughter Priyanka was equally eager to introduce her 'Nonna' (grandmother) to Diana.When Diana wondered why Sonia's mother was so quiet, Priyanka immediately explained that she had been told not to speak because she only knew Italian."Diana burst out laughing and turned immediately to my mother, holding out her hand, "Piacere, comne stai?" ("Pleased to meet you, how are you?"), trying to pronounce the words in the correct Italian accent, though using the informal form of address, but with such warmth and charm that we all melted," Sonia recalls.The meeting ended on another warm note. As the royal couple were leaving, Diana stopped midway, turned around and waved to Sonia's mother."After tea and more chat, we were seeing them off to their car when she stopped halfway, turned back to wave to my mother, and called out, 'Ciao. Nonna!' After I presented the royal couple with my book Rajiv, she wrote to me, telling me how much she had admired my husband," Sonia writes.Sonia also recounts a later meeting with Diana in London, when she was invited for tea with the royal couple. She remembers arriving in a black suit with a white collar and joking, "I am feeling like a crow!"On another occasion, she unexpectedly came across Diana at a hairdresser's. Recognising the princess sitting next to her, Sonia decided to pass her a discreet note."I scribbled a word and passed it on to her, and the next second realised that instead of 'Hi', I had written 'Hye'. How I wished I could have snatched back the note! But it was too late; she had already put it into her handbag," she recalls.The two exchanged a few words in hushed tones, careful not to attract attention. It was the last time Sonia met Diana.Reflecting on the public scrutiny surrounding the late princess, Sonia says Diana faced considerable criticism during her lifetime, with many questioning why she appeared unhappy despite her privileged position."There was a lot of criticism of her at that time: She was spoilt and complaining; she had everything; why was she behaving as if she had been wronged? I must say I felt for her throughout, and still do," Sonia writes.
Article Summary: Sonia Gandhi's memoir, Belonging: A Journey Of Love, is out now. She recalls her interactions with world leaders, including Bill Clinton and Princess Diana. She also recalls Nicolas Sarkozy's 2008 visit to India without his then partner, Carla Bruni.

Article Title: 'Unfortunate': Govt condemns anti-India campaign by Chinese vloggers, urges Bangladesh to take action

NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday condemned an alleged coordinated anti-India campaign by Chinese nationals who have reportedly been filming videos in slum areas of Dhaka for months and portraying the locations as parts of New Delhi during livestreams on Chinese social media platforms.During the weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal termed the incident as "unfortunate" and said that attempts to project a distorted picture of a country only undermine the credibility of those involved and those backing them."We have seen media reports in this regard. Such efforts to present a distorted picture of any country are unfortunate," Jaiswal said."Insofar as efforts to buy foreign elements to portray Dhaka as Delhi are concerned, the peddling of false narratives only undermines the credibility of those who are undertaking such actions and those who are behind them. And I would urge the authorities concerned to take action against such people," he added.According to recent media reports, Chinese vloggers and livestreamers have been recording videos in impoverished neighbourhoods of Dhaka, Bangladesh, while falsely identifying the locations as parts of New Delhi.The videos reportedly feature derogatory remarks about India's living conditions, sanitation, food habits and poverty.According to Prothom Alo, the activity has been reported in Sector 12 of Uttara and the adjoining Tekpara area of Dhaka, where local residents estimate that more than 150 Chinese nationals have been recording videos.The vloggers reportedly walk through streets and alleyways carrying two mobile phones, livestreaming for hours and, at times, entering people's homes to film. Their activities, which have continued for months, have increasingly angered residents, who remain unaware of where the footage is being published and how it is being presented.A Chinese national identified as Fangyou told Prothom Alo that the livestreams were part of product promotion activities on WeChat. A Bangladeshi woman, Ritu Akhter, who works as a guide for the Chinese nationals, said they also earned money by posting videos on platforms such as Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok."This is New Delhi. Their homes are extremely dirty. There isn't even a fan inside the tin-roofed houses. This place is quite underdeveloped, dirty and unhygienic, and the law-and-order situation is poor," she said.Apart from the misleading portrayal of their neighbourhoods, residents have raised concerns over repeated filming and alleged intrusions into their homes. Some claimed that the Chinese nationals entered houses and even bathrooms while recording."Sometimes they enter our homes and start filming. We are not always properly dressed inside our houses. Imagine how it feels when someone suddenly walks into your home and starts recording," resident Rozina Khatun told Prothom Alo.
Article Summary: Chinese vloggers and livestreamers have been recording videos in impoverished neighbourhoods of Dhaka, Bangladesh, while falsely identifying the locations as parts of New Delhi. The videos reportedly feature derogatory remarks about India's living conditions, sanitation, food habits and poverty. Residents have raised concerns over repeated filming and alleged intrusions into their homes.

NEW DELHI: An unknown gunman shot dead Mohammad Sharif , an accused linked to the 2008 CRPF camp attack, on Tuesday. Sharif was killed in Rampur, UP with bystanders alleging he was shot 16 times. The police have initiated a manhunt for the shooter/s.Seven CRPF personnel and a rickshaw puller were killed in a pre-dawn terror attack, plotted by Lashkar-e-Taiba , on the CRPF Group Centre in Rampur on the night of December 31, 2007-Jan 1, 2008. In May 2025, unknown gunmen had killed Abu Saifullah Khalid, a key Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) operative and the mastermind behind the 2006 RSS headquarters attack and multiple terror strikes, including one on a CRPF camp in Uttar Pradesh.Sharif, who belonged to Badanpuri-Khajuria village in Rampur, went by aliases of Suhail, Sajid, Anwar and Ali, according to police records. He was lodged in Bareilly central jail and released last Nov.Arrested in the case in the aftermath of the attack, a UP court had in 2019 convicted Sharif and five others including two Pakistani nationals in the case. Four including Sharif were subsequently sentenced to death after they were found directly involved in the attack.In Oct 2025, the Allahabad High Court, however, overturned the death sentences but upheld their conviction under the Arms Act for possessing prohibited weapons, sentencing them to ten years’ rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 1 lakh each. The HC had noted procedural lapses by the police like failure to conduct a Test Identification Parade (TIP) and also found lapses in the handling of physical evidence, observing that firearms, cartridges, and grenades allegedly recovered from the scene were not securely preserved or properly traced through the chain of custody. Key witnesses who should have verified storage and transfer of evidence were not examined.
Article Summary: Sharif was killed in Rampur, UP with bystanders alleging he was shot 16 times. The police have initiated a manhunt for the shooter/s. Seven CRPF personnel and a rickshaw puller were killed in a pre-dawn terror attack, plotted by Lashkar-e- Taiba.

NEW DELHI: What began withhas grown into one of the world's largest vaccination drives. Now, smallpox is history, polio has been eliminated, and maternal and neonatal tetanus are no longer public health threats in India.That's quite a flex!India's vaccination story is one of ambitious campaigns, millions of doses and some remarkable public health victories. The country was declared polio-free in 2014. A year later, it eliminated maternal and neonatal tetanus as a public health problem. Then, during the Covid-19 pandemic, it administered over 200 crore vaccine doses, including indigenously developed and licensed vaccines manufactured in India.And the drive is far from over.Earlier this year, the government added another shot to India's public health armoury with a nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign for 14-year-old girls, aimed at protecting them against cervical cancer. It also launched an indigenously manufactured tetanus-diphtheria (Td) vaccine. From fighting childhood infections to preventing cancer,India's vaccine drive is continuously levelling up. According to the Union health ministry, full immunisation coverage climbed from 62% in 2015 to 98.4% in January 2026.Last year, the figure stood at 97.9%.However, there is still a long way to go.Lakhs of children are missing essential shots with coverage remaining uneven across states. At the same time, many older adults are still largely missing from the vaccination picture.But if India has come this far, why are so many people still missing their shots?India's vaccination story goes back more than two centuries. The first smallpox vaccination in the country was administered in Mumbai on June 14, 1802, after vaccine lymph arrived from abroad. Nearly a century later, in 1897, Dr Waldemar Haffkine developed India's first indigenous vaccine against plague, also in Bombay.The government's efforts to make immunisation more organised gathered pace in 1962 with the launch of the national BCG programme to control tuberculosis. This was followed by the Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) in 1978, which marked another step towards wider vaccine coverage.However, 1985 proved to be a bigger turning point. India launched the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP), bringing free vaccines against 12 preventable diseases to children and pregnant women. The initiative laid the foundation for what has since grown into one of the world's largest publicly funded vaccination programmes.The scale of the operation today is enormous. Every year, the UIP reaches 2.9 crore pregnant women and 2.54 crore newborns every year, free of cost . A vast network of government healthcare centres, frontline health workers, cold-chain facilities and digital systems supports the delivery and tracking of these doses.The programme's vaccine basket has also grown over the years. What initially focused on diseases such as tuberculosis, polio and tetanus now offers protection against a wider range of infections, including rotavirus diarrhoea, rubella and serious illnesses caused by pneumococcal bacteria.Alongside this expansion came some major public health victories. India eliminated smallpox, yaws, polio and maternal and neonatal tetanus as public health threats. Immunisation has also contributed to lower child mortality and reduced the burden of diseases such as measles and rubella.One campaign, in particular, became a defining moment in this journey. Launched in 1995, the Pulse Polio Programme took vaccination beyond healthcare centres and turned it into a nationwide public movement. Its now-familiar slogan,, helped bring millions of people into the campaign. The last reported case of wild polio in India was recorded on January 13, 2011, in Howrah, West Bengal. In 2014, the country was certified polio-free.But maintaining high vaccination coverage is an ongoing exercise. Full immunisation coverage stood at 94.7% in 2022-23, slipped to 93.7% in 2023-24, rose to 98.3% in 2024-25 and eased to 97.9% in 2025-26.India has also made progress in reaching children who have not received any routine vaccines, commonly referred to as zero-dose children. Their share declined from 0.11% in 2023 to 0.06% in 2024.Vaccination is not a one-and-done exercise. Some shots are given at birth, others follow at carefully spaced intervals, and a few need boosters to keep protection going. But what exactly do these jabs do?A vaccine essentially prepares the immune system for an encounter with a disease-causing germ. It teaches the body to recognise the threat and respond faster if it comes into contact with it later. This reduces the risk of infection and, in many cases, prevents severe illness.In India, this protection begins at birth. Newborns receive vaccines against tuberculosis (BCG), polio and hepatitis B. The hepatitis B birth dose is particularly time-sensitive and should ideally be administered within the first 24 hours.The next round begins when the baby is six weeks old, with follow-up doses at ten and fourteen weeks. These vaccines protect against diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, hepatitis B, polio, rotavirus diarrhoea and infections caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib).Pneumococcal vaccines are also included in the schedule to protect infants against serious infections, including certain types of pneumonia and meningitis.The vaccination calendar does not stop once babies become toddlers. Between nine and 12 months, children receive their first measles-rubella dose, followed by a second at 16-24 months. Japanese encephalitis vaccines are also offered in endemic districts.As children get older, booster doses become part of the routine. DPT boosters are given during early childhood, followed by tetanus-diphtheria (Td) shots at the ages of ten and 16 to maintain protection.The schedule is also expanding beyond childhood infections, with cancer prevention entering the picture.On February 28, 2026, the government launched a nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign, offering a free, voluntary, single-dose vaccine to around 1.2 crore girls aged 14. The campaign aims to protect them against HPV infections that can lead to cervical cancer.The rollout has gathered pace, too. By September 11, more than 80 lakh doses had been administered, with Uttar Pradesh accounting for the highest number at over 22 lakh.From a newborn's first vaccines to an adolescent's HPV shot, India's immunisation schedule covers several stages of life. But having vaccines on the calendar is only half the job. Ensuring that every eligible beneficiary receives the right dose at the right time remains the bigger challenge.The latest WHO-UNICEF estimates for 2025 suggest that India is making steady progress in getting more children vaccinated. Around 97% received the first dose of the diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTP) vaccine, while 95% completed all three doses. Measles vaccination coverage was equally encouraging, with 98% of children receiving the first dose and 95% getting the second.There is another milestone worth celebrating. The number of zero-dose children, those who have not received even the first dose of a DTP-containing vaccine, fell from around 9.09 lakh in 2024 to 6.79 lakh in 2025. That's a decline of nearly 25% in just one year.India also achieved a significant first. For the first time since WHO-UNICEF estimates began in 2001, it dropped out of the world's top ten countries with the highest number of children missing measles vaccination.In this case, slipping down the rankings is actually good news!However, the progress is not uniform. WHO's 2025 estimates show that only 70% of newborns received the hepatitis B birth dose within 24 hours, while rotavirus vaccine coverage stood at 91%.India has made steady progress towards universal immunisation, with full vaccination coverage among children aged 12-23 months rising from 83.8% to 87.1%, according to vaccination card records.The household survey also brings out a gap that national averages can easily mask: differences between states. Full vaccination coverage among children aged 12-23 months ranged from 93.8% in Goa to just 64.3% in Nagaland, a gap of nearly 30 percentage points.The divide is visible in hepatitis B vaccination, too. While 91.9% of newborns in Goa received the birth dose, the figure was only 46.4% in Nagaland.In other words, India's vaccination report card may be improving, but the marks are far from evenly distributed. Where a child is born can still make a significant difference to the protection they receive.So, if childhood vaccines are free, why are so many children still missing their shots?The answer lies in barriers that go beyond the availability of vaccines. From caregiver hesitation to migration and poor access to healthcare, several factors can leave children partially or completely unvaccinated.A WHO report from April 2026 offers some insight. Under its TrackVac initiative, the vaccination status of 2,24,698 children was assessed across 143 priority districts in 11 states during 2025. Among children who remained unvaccinated, caregiver refusal accounted for 39% of cases, while migration was responsible for 34%.While these findings are based on targeted districts and do not represent a nationwide survey, they highlight two major hurdles in India's immunisation efforts: vaccine hesitancy and disruptions in access to healthcare.Migration, in particular, can interrupt a child's vaccination schedule. A family moving from one city to another for work may get its baby the first dose but miss subsequent appointments after relocating. In remote villages and underserved urban settlements, long distances, transport costs, limited awareness and the loss of a day's wages can also discourage families from returning for the next dose.Misinformation and fears about side effects add to the challenge. With several vaccines requiring multiple doses, missing even one appointment can leave a child only partially protected.The challenge, therefore, is not just to make vaccines free but also to ensure that families can access them easily, understand their importance and complete the recommended vaccination schedule.For many Indians, the vaccination chapter quietly ends with school, but adults need those shots too!Depending on age, health and vaccination history, adults may benefit from vaccines against influenza, pneumococcal disease, hepatitis B, shingles and other infections.Tetanus-diphtheria boosters still matter, and pregnant women receive tetanus-diphtheria vaccination under India's public immunisation programme. Older adults and people with chronic health conditions face higher risks from certain infections, so age-appropriate vaccination is especially relevant for them.Yet adult vaccination has mostly stayed in the shadows. According to an earlier TOI report, citing older Longitudinal Ageing Study in India data, highlighted strikingly low uptake among older Indians: just 1.59% had received the influenza vaccine, 0.74% the pneumococcal vaccine, 1.82% the hepatitis B vaccine, and 2.75% the tetanus-diphtheria vaccine. These are historical survey figures rather than fresh 2026 measurements, but they show how thin adult coverage has been.India's Covid-19 campaign, which delivered more than 220 crore doses, proved that mass adult immunisation can be done. Yet unlike childhood vaccination, there's still no comparable universal routine programme for older adults.But things are starting to change.In September 2026, Goa became India's first state to adopt a dedicated life-course immunisation policy for 2026-2036, initially focusing on influenza, pneumococcal and hepatitis B vaccines for eligible high-risk adults.Turns out vaccination isn't just a childhood routing but also needs to continue well into adulthood.Finding children who have missed their vaccines is only half the battle. Ensuring they receive every due dose on time remains the bigger challenge.The government has stepped up efforts to close this gap through initiatives such as Mission Indradhanush, which has vaccinated over 5.46 crore children and 1.32 crore pregnant women. The U-WIN portal, which had 11.87 crore children registered as of March 2026, is another step towards better tracking, helping health workers monitor vaccination schedules and send reminders for missed doses.WHO's TrackVac initiative also highlights how targeted follow-ups can make a difference. About 85% of the children whose records were verified were already listed in health workers' registers, while 53% were subsequently vaccinated.However, migration, misinformation and vaccine hesitancy continue to pose challenges, making community outreach and regular follow-ups just as important as vaccine availability.The challenge does not end with just childhood immunisation.Limited awareness, high costs and poor access continue to hold back adult vaccination, particularly among senior citizens. Experts call for India-specific adult immunisation guidelines, with routine vaccination against influenza, pneumococcal disease, shingles and tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis, as well as hepatitis B shots for high-risk groups.Clearly, closing the vaccination gap will require more than free doses and digital records. Timely follow-ups, better awareness and easier access must go hand in hand to ensure people do not miss out on protection.The goal is to make vaccination a lifelong priority, not just a childhood routine.
Article Summary: India's vaccination story goes back more than two centuries. The first smallpox vaccination in the country was administered in Mumbai on June 14, 1802. Now, smallpox is history, polio has been eliminated, and maternal and neonatal tetanus are no longer public health threats in India.

Article Title: Nearly 77% foreign medical graduates fail FMGE; only 9,354 clear screening test

NEW DELHI: Nearly four out of five foreign medical graduates (FMGs) who appeared for the October 2026 Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE), mandatory for foreign-trained doctors seeking to practise in India, failed to qualify. Only 9,354 candidates passed, against 31,539 who failed, taking the pass percentage to 22.9%.The results come after months of protests by foreign medical graduates over the June examination, following which the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) announced a series of measures based on an expert committee's recommendations. The October 31 examination was scheduled as an additional session to give candidates another opportunity to qualify.The committee had recommended a question-paper difficulty distribution of 30% easy, 50% moderate and 20% difficult questions. It also proposed allowing candidates to view their recorded responses, correct answers and marks awarded for individual questions.However, Dr Samar Kumar, National FMG In-charge, FAIMA, said feedback from candidates suggested that the October paper was moderate to difficult and did not appear to follow the recommended difficulty ratio.He said the October pass percentage of 22.86% was comparable to previous December-January sessions, while the June 2026 pass rate had fallen to around 12%. The absence of video-based questions in October may have contributed to the improvement, he said, as candidates had found them unfamiliar and time-consuming in June.Kumar also flagged the lack of clarity over the promised answer key, distant exam centres and late admit cards, which caused anxiety among candidates. He welcomed the fee reduction but urged NBEMS to clarify its commitments and ensure greater transparency.The results, declared by NBEMS on Tuesday, showed that of the 42,113 candidates listed, 1,190 were absent and the results of 30 candidates were withheld.An analysis of the score list showed that 14,613 candidates scored between 125 and 149 marks out of 300 but failed to meet the qualifying threshold of 150. Of these, 5,365 scored between 140 and 149, falling just short of the required marks.Candidates who qualify must undergo in-person identity and credential verification to receive their FMGE pass certificates. NBEMS said the reasons for withholding 30 candidates’ results had been communicated by email. Individual scorecards will be available from November 20 for six months, but cannot be used for registration with State Medical Councils in place of the pass certificate.NBEMS said subject experts reviewed all questions, awarding marks for technically incorrect questions and either accepted answer. Results remain provisional, and candidature may be cancelled if a candidate is found ineligible, even after the result or pass certificate is issued.
Article Summary: Only 9,354 candidates passed, against 31,539 who failed, taking the pass percentage to 22.9%. The results come after months of protests by foreign medical graduates over the June examination. The October 31 examination was scheduled as an additional session to give candidates another opportunity to qualify.
